And Athens and Sparta are both Greek, but they're different societies. In fact, they're nothing alike. First of all, Sparta is on flat land. The Peloponnesians settled there. If you're on flat land, you can use agriculture, but to do so, you need slaves. So Sparta became a war society that conquered the surrounding people and turned them into slaves called helots. These helots were farm slaves. Thus, Sparta's society centered around military dominance. They focused on turning young boys into great warriors to defend their land.

The Spartans were also very conservative because maintaining control over the helots was their primary concern. If they went to conquer other places, the helots could rebel against them. Think of China for a comparison. As a result, Sparta was an oligarchy, ruled by the few. Only Spartans born to both Spartan parents were citizens; everyone else was not. Even if your father was Spartan but your mother was not, you were not a citizen.

There's a massive class hierarchy in Sparta because maintaining the status quo was their priority. In contrast, the Athenians didn't have good farmland but had a good harbor. Their territory was mountainous, unsuitable for growing crops except olives. So, they had to be expansionist, building a strong navy and focusing on trade and piracy.

Spartans were conservative while the Athenians were open and expansionist. If you're in a navy, you need to be a democracy. In Greece, fighting for your country allowed you to vote and participate in politics. Sparta was an oligarchy due to its land army with hoplites, whereas Athens was a democracy because of its navy where everyone could participate.

Over time, as Athens expanded democratically, Sparta's power waned, leading to conflict during the Peloponnesian War. Eventually, these three states—Athens, Thebes, and Sparta—reached an equilibrium. Similar to the Warring States period in China, they used war to resolve domestic tensions.

A new power arose called Macedonia, taking military innovations from Sparta, Athens, and Thebes. Philip II of Macedon was a great military genius but is less remembered due to his son, Alexander the Great, who conquered Persia using these innovations. As this system reached equilibrium, a new power rose—Rome—and we'll discuss that next class.

Alexander will conquer the Persian Empire, showing how this pattern repeats throughout history.
